sections.html:
A Louisiana eviction is a fast, summary court case that starts only after a written notice to vacate has gone unanswered. The steps follow the Code of Civil Procedure, title XI, which governs the eviction of tenants and occupants.

  1. The lessor or owner delivers a written notice to vacate (art. 4701 or 4702).
  2. If the tenant or occupant does not comply, the owner has the court cite them to appear by a rule to show cause why possession should not be delivered (art. 4731). The rule states the grounds.
  3. The court makes the rule returnable no earlier than the third day after service, tries it and hears any defense (art. 4732(A)).
  4. If the owner wins, or the tenant fails to answer or appear, the court renders a judgment of eviction immediately (art. 4732(B)).
  5. If the tenant has not complied within twenty-four hours, the court issues a warrant to its sheriff, constable or marshal to deliver possession to the owner (art. 4733).

Our companion guide on the eviction notice covers step one in detail. This page starts at the courthouse.

A justice of the peace court can hear a residential eviction, and so can the parish or district court. Code of Civil Procedure art. 4912 gives justice of the peace courts jurisdiction, shared with the parish or district court, over suits by landowners or lessors to evict occupants or tenants of leased residential premises, whatever the monthly or yearly rent.

The article also reaches some commercial and farm leases. A justice of the peace court may hear evictions of tenants of leased commercial premises and farmland where monthly rent does not exceed $5,000, again regardless of the rent due or the rent for the rest of the lease.

Which courthouse an owner uses depends on where the house sits. In a parish with city courts, parish courts or justice of the peace wards, the clerk of court can tell you where an eviction rule is filed.

The statute sets short minimum windows, and real calendars depend on the court. These are the numbers to plan around.

Statutory time limits in a Louisiana eviction
StageTime allowed
Notice to vacate (art. 4701)At least 5 days from delivery
Hearing on the rule (art. 4732(A))Not earlier than the third day after service
Judgment of eviction (art. 4732(B))Effective for not less than 90 days
Voluntary compliance (art. 4733)Within 24 hours of the judgment
Suspensive appeal request and bond (art. 4735)Within 24 hours of the judgment

Add up the minimums and the fastest lawful path takes more than a week from delivery of the notice. That assumes the owner files promptly and the court has an open hearing slot.

The judge tries the rule on the day it is returnable and hears any defense the tenant raises. Bring the lease if there is one, the written notice with proof of when it was delivered, and a record of what is owed.

A tenant who fails to answer or appear loses by default. Under art. 4732(B), the court renders a judgment of eviction immediately if the owner is entitled to relief or the lessee or occupant fails to answer or appear. That judgment is effective for not less than ninety days, which gives the owner time to carry out the order rather than a single day.

Owners who are family members, heirs or buyers should bring documents showing they now hold the lessor's position. Art. 4704 defines lessor to include an assignee or transferee, so title paperwork matters.

Yes, but an appeal does not stop the eviction by itself. Under art. 4735, execution of the judgment is suspended only if the defendant answered the rule under oath pleading an affirmative defense that would entitle them to keep possession, applied for the appeal, and filed the appeal bond within twenty-four hours after the judgment.

The court sets the amount of the suspensive appeal bond, enough to protect the appellee against damage from the appeal. For the owner, that twenty-four hour window usually decides whether the warrant for possession can issue.

sections.h2: What a landlord cannot do during an eviction
sections.html:
An owner who skips the court process risks a penalty. Under art. 4731(C)(2), a lessor's failure to follow that article lets a residential lessee recover $500 or twice the monthly rent, whichever is greater, and the tenant may seek a restraining order or injunction. The court may award costs and attorney fees to the prevailing party.

After a federally declared disaster, the same article adds thirty days of protection for residents of the declared parishes: a household that has left the home is not treated as having abandoned it during that time. For a Louisiana seller whose rental was hit by a hurricane or flood, that affects whether the house can be treated as vacant.

sections.h2: Does selling a rented house end the lease?
sections.html:
No. Civil Code art. 2711 provides that transfer of the leased thing does not terminate the lease unless the lessor and lessee agreed otherwise. The buyer arrives with the tenant already in the house.

Whether the buyer is bound by the lease turns on recording. Under art. 2712, a third person who acquires an immovable subject to an unrecorded lease is not bound by it, and the lessee, absent a contrary clause in the lease, has an action against the lessor for losses caused by the transfer. R.S. 9:2721 goes the other way for recorded leases: a buyer of property subject to a recorded lease that is not divested by the acquisition takes the property subject to all its provisions, including any provision for paying a commission to a leasing agent.

Before listing, find out whether the lease was ever recorded in the parish conveyance records, and what it says about rent, term and early termination.

sections.h2: The tenant's security deposit in a sale
sections.html:
The deposit moves with the property. Under R.S. 9:3251(B), when the lessor's interest is transferred during the lease, the transferor must also transfer the deposit to the successor, and the transferor is then relieved of further liability for it. The new owner becomes responsible for returning it when the lease ends.

The general rule in subsection (A) requires return to a residential tenant within one month after the lease ends. The landlord may keep what is reasonably needed to remedy a default or unreasonable wear, and if any is kept, an itemized statement with reasons is due within that month. The tenant must give a forwarding address, and the one-month rule does not apply where the tenant abandons the premises.

Write the deposit amount into the sale paperwork so it is credited correctly at closing.

It depends on the lease, the case and how much time you have. Finishing the eviction clears the house for showings, but it takes court time and may mean cleanup of what the tenant leaves behind.

Owners weighing the choice usually compare:

  • Cost and time of finishing a case, including repairs after the tenant leaves.
  • Whether the lease is recorded and would bind a buyer under R.S. 9:2721.
  • Whether the tenant is paying and wants to stay, which changes the picture entirely.
  • A sale as-is with the tenant in place, which passes the lease and the deposit to the buyer under the rules above.

We also look at houses that come with tenants or a difficult rental history. A Louisiana attorney can advise on a specific lease.

faqs.q: How long does a Louisiana eviction take after the notice period?
faqs.a: The court may set the hearing no earlier than the third day after service of the rule. If the owner wins, the tenant has twenty-four hours to comply before a warrant issues. Actual timing depends on the court's calendar.

faqs.q: Which court handles evictions in Louisiana?
faqs.a: Justice of the peace courts share jurisdiction with parish or district courts over residential evictions under art. 4912, whatever the rent.

faqs.q: How long is a Louisiana judgment of eviction good for?
faqs.a: At least ninety days, under art. 4732(B). That gives the owner time to obtain a warrant and have possession delivered.

faqs.q: Does an appeal stop a Louisiana eviction?
faqs.a: Only in narrow cases. The tenant must have answered under oath pleading an affirmative defense, and must apply for the appeal and file the bond within twenty-four hours of the judgment.

faqs.q: Does the lease end if I sell my rented Louisiana house?
faqs.a: No. Civil Code art. 2711 says transfer of the leased thing does not terminate the lease unless the parties agreed otherwise. A recorded lease binds the buyer under R.S. 9:2721, while an unrecorded lease does not bind a third-party buyer under art. 2712.
